inline.s: The Sixth Year, Renshen (1573).

I was twenty-seven. I had just reached Yangzhou when heavy snow blocked the way and illness came upon me. After a long while I begged for food in the market, yet could not get past the first door. Wondering why, I quickly asked myself and said: It is because I still have two mace of silver wrapped at my waist, and so I lean on that. Thereupon I saw monks and Daoists in the snow who had begged in vain, and I invited them all into a tavern; I threw in the silver, and it was spent in a single meal. The next day I went out into the street and entered a door or two, and was able to call out — so I got food. Then I rejoiced and said: My own strength is enough to make ten thousand bushels of rank seem light. I inscribed my bowl: A vessel that makes ten thousand bushels light. I inscribed my robe: A garment that makes the whole world light. And I made an inscription for them, saying: You entrust me with form; I entrust you with mind. Thus this one body is indeed made sufficient by it, while the ten thousand things are truly made light through it. Soon I shall trail the sleeves of the long wind and wear the lapel of white clouds. When I rise, it is like the wings of a swan; when I rest, it is like the scales of a hidden dragon. I wander free through the universe, going and staying among the mountains and forests. What use have I to flaunt the splendor of scarlet and purple? I prize only what frost and snow cannot invade. In the seventh month of that autumn I arrived at the capital, with not a foot of ground to stand on. I begged all day and got nothing. At dusk I came to the tea shed of the West Taiping Granary and got only one meal. I put up for the night at the Yi Jiao Temple by the Grand Canal. The next day Zuo Sima Wang Boyu, learning that I had come, invited me — because he was a sworn friend of his younger brother Zhongyan. Thus I found lodging. Within ten days I paid my respects to Dharma Master Mohe and went with him to the Western Hills to hear the Miaozong Chao. There is a poem of mine, Longing for My Elder Brother at the Western Hills. When the lecture term ended, Mohe kept me through the winter to hear the Lotus Sutra and the Consciousness-Only teachings, and asked Dharma Master An to explain the three-part syllogism of Hetuvidya. In the eleventh month Master Miaofeng came seeking me. The Master had grown a long beard and wore coarse cloth. He first announced: A salt merchant has come to call. When he entered, the Master at once asked: Do you still know me? I looked at him closely; seeing his two eyes, I suddenly recalled the sick latrine-cleaner of former days at Tianjie Temple. So I said: I know you. The Master said: I have changed my face and head. I replied: The original face abides of itself. We smiled at each other, with no leisure to speak of other things. He only asked where I lodged. I said: Longhua; I shall come to see you tomorrow. That night as we sat, I asked how it was with him. Why was he thus? The Master said: Because I long dwelt in the mountains, my hair grew long and uncut. It happened that a benefactor, the Prince of Shanyin, was building a monastery and sent for the Inner Canon, and so I came. He asked after my circumstances, and I said: I came especially to seek the Master, and also to view the capital and call on the wise, so as to cut off the idle thoughts of days to come. The Master said: Since we parted I have thought of you without cease, and feared we had no affinity. Now happily you have come. I am willing to accompany you, begging, and to go ahead of you to drive off the dogs. We talked the whole night; at daybreak we smiled and parted. I then went to call on Great Master Bianrong. I bowed and begged the Elder for instruction. The Master was silent, only gazing straight at me. I called on Master Xiaoyan. He asked: Where have you come from? I said: From the south. He asked: Do you remember the road by which you came? I said: Once past, and it is done. The Master said: Then your place of coming is clear. I bowed, stood in attendance and sought instruction; the Master gave a few words on the upward matter and I took my leave.
The First Year of Wanli, Guiyou (1573).

I was twenty-eight. In the first month of spring I set out to roam Mount Wutai. First I sought the Record of Clear and Cool, and traced its sites. At the North Peak I saw a place called Hanshan, and asked where that mountain was; a monk pointed it out. It was indeed wonderfully beautiful, and I silently took it as my name; a poem records it — Let them go as they will; here I shall rest the working of the mind. Because I could not bear the bitter cold of ice and snow, I could not stay. I went east of the capital to wander again, and begging my way I reached Mount Pan. In the stone chamber of the Thousand Images Valley I met a monk who did not speak, and I asked nothing either; we simply gathered firewood, drew water and begged together. Sima Wang sent a letter seeking me, saying: I fear you have become a starving man of the eastern suburbs. When autumn came I returned to the capital, because the Lingnan scholar Ou Zhenbo, who years before had sent me a letter though we had never met, was now an Erudite of the Court and urgently wished to see me.
The Second Year, Jiaxu (1574).

I was twenty-nine. That spring I roamed the Western Hills of the capital. The famous men of the day — the two Wangs, the two Wangs of the Secretariat, and Ou Zhenbo of Nanhai — were all gathered at the capital. One day I called on Wang Fenzhou. When we met he took me lightly because of my youth, and I bore myself proudly as guest before host. At once he earnestly instructed me in the method of composing poetry. I stared at him wide-eyed and in the end took my leave without a single word. He was displeased and spoke of it to his younger brother Wang Linshou. The next day Linshou came to visit me; at the first sight he said: Last night my elder brother lost one eye. I said: Have you the one eye, sir? He bowed with clasped hands and said: This youngster has seen it. Laughing together, we returned. He told his brother: Elder brother, you have lost to Vimalakirti. So he gave me a poem, with the lines: One may know that Wang Yishao yielded the subtle doctrine to Master Zhi. One day the younger Wang, living in the same place as I, read the Zuo Commentary, and said to me: Your natural gifts are extraordinary and you have greatly the spirit of letters. My uncle is the literary master of the age — why do you not take him as your teacher and make a name for yourself as a writer? I laughed and spat, saying: Keep your knee, elder brother, and one day you shall bow to this old monk and receive the meaning of the coming from the West. Linshou was much displeased and reported it to Sima Wang. The Duke said: Truly so. I observe that Yigong has the bone of the Way; one day he will enter the room of Dahui and Zhongfeng. How could he be content with mere letters? Only I fear he will go astray in idle wandering. Seeing a poem of mine written on a fan together with Linshou's — with the lines: This body and world, two wings of a cicada; heaven and earth, one hair of a horse — he showed it to Linshou and said: Can this be a monk of letters? One day he made a vegetarian feast especially to invite me, and I sat together with Master Miao. The Duke said to me: The Chan gate lies desolate, and it is greatly to be feared. This youngster thinks of it earnestly. By your bearing, sir, your future achievement will not be small. Why do you waste yourself in wandering? I said: This poor monk came especially for the sake of the great matter, to call on the wise. Now I only wish to survey the men of the age and so be done with the idle thoughts of days to come. It is no idle wandering. And soon I shall be going. The Duke said: Truly. I observe that in these times there is none fit to be your teacher. Were it not for Miaofeng, you would have no friend. I said: Long ago I marked him out among the crowd and we made a pact to train together; that is why I came north to seek him. I did not expect to meet him here by chance. The Duke said: How strange! If you two truly go, this youngster wishes to ferry you across. At that time Master Miao had brought back the canon, so Sima Wang gave us two travel warrants, and also wrote a piece to see me off. One day the Duke summoned me in haste and asked: Miaofeng has gone. Why did you not take leave of him? I said: Let him go slowly. The Duke said: I know you do not wish to turn on another's heel. But that is quite wrong. The ancients were not ashamed of small proprieties, but ashamed that their merit and name should not be shown to the world. I only hope that one day you will accomplish a work of light for the Dharma gate. Why then weigh comings and goings so narrowly? I was moved, bowed in thanks, and resolved to go. I went at once to see Master Miao; he had already loaded his cart. Seeing me come, he asked: Are you going, Master? I said: I am going. He mounted the cart, and we left without taking leave of anyone. In the eighth month of autumn we crossed Mengjin and saw the place where King Wu reviewed his troops; I wrote a poem in lament, with the lines: A slab of stone, a ruined stele, leaning at the river's head; here in that year he once gathered the feudal lords. The royal order he would make to last as heaven and earth: it should flow on with the Yellow River, unbroken. Passing the place where Boyi and Shuqi held back the horse, I lamented: Casting off the state and its glory, their purpose was already deep; there remains only the ancient shrine, its cypresses dense and dark. How clear are the colors of Mount Shouyang — still the very heart that held back the horse in that year. Then I entered Shaolin and paid my respects to the First Patriarch. At that time Master Qianrun had just entered the monastery; I sought him but did not meet him. Leaving the mountain, I saw the ancient city of Luoyang, the Terrace Where the Sutras Were Burned, and the White Horse Temple. Then I followed after Master Miao. In the ninth month I reached Hedong, where I met Shanyin, and so stayed to spend the winter. Then Prefect Chen invited Master Miao and me, his intention most earnest, and had the Zhongwu Collected Exegesis of the Zhao Lun carved. I collated it. Previously I had not understood the purport of the passage in the Treatise on Not Moving — the whirlwind stills the peaks — and had long harbored doubt in secret. Now that I came to it, I was still bewildered. Then I came to the passage where the Brahmin left home in youth and returned white-haired, and a neighbor seeing him said: Is the man of former days still here? The Brahmin said: I am like the man of former days, but I am not the man of former days. Suddenly I understood and said: Truly, all dharmas are without coming or going. At once I came down from the meditation bed and bowed to the Buddha, and there was no sign of rising or moving. I lifted the blind and stood before the steps; suddenly the wind blew the courtyard trees and flying leaves filled the sky, and there was no sign of motion. I said: This is the whirlwind stilling the peaks and forever quiet. When I later went out to the privy, there was no sign of flowing. I said: This is the rivers racing on and yet not flowing. Thereupon the doubt of coming and going, of birth and death, melted away like ice. So I had a verse: Birth and death are night and day; the water flows, the flowers fall. Today at last I know the nostrils turn downward. The next day Master Miao met me and said joyfully: What have you attained, Master? I said: Last night I saw two iron oxen by the river, fighting as they went into the water; to this day there is no news of them. The Master laughed and said: I am glad you have the capital to dwell in the mountains. Before long Shanyin invited the Chan Master Faguang of Mount Niu to come. I had long admired him, and when we met I rejoiced to sit in practice with him. Our words met in the vital turn; I sought instruction, and he opened to me: Investigate apart from mind, intellect and consciousness; study beyond the paths of the ordinary and the sage. I deeply grasped his purport. Whenever I heard the Master speak, it was like the sound of a heavenly drum. Then I knew that one who has awakened and made clear the ground of mind indeed speaks and breathes differently. I was deeply devoted to him. One day he searched my bag, found my poems and read them, and sighed: Such fine lines — whence did you get them? Then he laughed: Fine they are, but that one aperture is still not open. I asked: Is the Master's aperture open? He said: Thirty years I have seized dragons and caught tigers; today a rabbit runs out of the grass and startles me. I said: The Master is no dragon-seizer or tiger-catcher. He picked up his staff and was about to strike; I caught it, stroked his beard with my hand and said: You say it is a rabbit; it is just a toad. He laughed and let the matter drop. One day he said: You need not go elsewhere. I would have you grow old with me on Mount Funiu — that is my hope. I said: By the Master's Dharma eloquence in debate you are not less than Dahui. Yet in daily life you seem to have the manner of a madman, forever humming and mumbling without pause — why is that? The Master said: That is my Chan sickness. When I first awakened, verses poured like a stream, day and night without cease; I could not stop them, and so it became an illness. I said: When this illness first arose, how should it have been treated? The Master said: When this illness breaks out, if you cannot see through it yourself, you must get a man of great eye and great hand to give you a sound beating and make you sleep soundly; when you wake, it will vanish of itself. I only regret that I had no ruthless hand. At the year's end the Master knew I would go to Wutai at the New Year, and sent me off with a poem, with the lines: The lion in the clouds, ride it here to see; the hidden dragon in the cave, let it go and rest. He asked: Do you understand? I said: I do not. The Master said: I want you not to grasp a dead snake. I nodded. For long the Chan way had had no master craftsman; when I met Master Guang, I first knew that the school of Chan has its strategies. The Prince of Shanyin asked whether my parents were living, and gave me two hundred pieces of gold for their support in old age. I declined, saying: This poor monk has just begun his pilgrimage and cannot yet save himself; how would I dare burden my parents? So I yielded it to Master Guang.
The Third Year, Yihai (1575).

I was thirty. In the first month I went up Mount Wutai from Hedong together with Master Miao, passing through Pingyang, the Master's home country. The Master's family had been poor in his youth, and in a year of famine his parents died; there was nothing to bury them in. So Shanyin and a few officials helped, and I chose a high, open plot for a joint burial and wrote the grave record. The Master's secular surname was Xu; the family lived in the eastern suburb of Pingyang, descendants, it seems, of Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period. Prefect Hu, styled Shun'an, a man of Donglai, heard that I had arrived and lodged outside the city; he wished to see me but could not. When I set out, the Duke sent me a travel warrant. I said: A man of the Way on pilgrimage has only his straw sandals — what need has he of this? The Duke esteemed me the more. When I had gone, he followed after me; at Lingshi we finally met, and went together to the provincial capital, where he kept me in talk for several days and sent servants to escort me to Mount Tai. On the fifteenth of the second month I lodged at Tayuan Temple. The host Dafang chose for me a dwelling at Longmen on the North Peak, the most secluded and precipitous of places. On the third day of the third month I cleared out a few rafters of an old hut from the snowdrifts and lived there. At that time I saw ten thousand mountains of ice and snow — exactly the realm I had long admired. Body and mind were washed clean, as though I had entered the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Before long Miaofeng left to roam Yedai, and I dwelt there alone, holding to a single thought. When people came I did not speak, only looked at them. After a long time I saw people as stumps, until I reached the place where not one word is known. At first great winds would rise and ten thousand apertures howled; ice melted and the mountain streams rushed and surged like thunder. In the stillness I heard sounds like a thousand armies and ten thousand horses setting out, and found it a great clamor. So I asked Master Miao. He said: The realm arises from the mind; it does not come from outside. I have heard the ancients say: Hear the sound of water for thirty years without turning the faculty of mind, and you shall realize Guanyin's perfect penetration. There was a single-log bridge over the stream; day after day I sat and stood upon it. At first the sound of water was clear and distinct; after a long time, when a thought stirred I heard it, and when no thought stirred I did not. One day as I sat on the bridge I suddenly forgot my body, and the sound was utterly still. From then on all sounds were still and no longer disturbed me. I ate wheat bran mixed with wild greens each day, sending it down with a broth of a little rice. At first people sent me three pecks of rice; half a year later there was still some left. One day after the gruel, as I walked in meditation, I suddenly stood still: body and mind were gone, and there was only one great treasury of radiance, perfect, still and serene, like a great perfect mirror, in which the mountains, rivers and great earth appeared as reflections. When I came to, all was bright and clear; I sought my body and mind and could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: In one flash a single thought — the mad mind rests; within and without, faculties and dust are wholly clear. I turn and break through the great empty space; the myriad forms in dense array arise and cease. From then on within and without were serene, and no sound, voice, form or appearance obstructed me any more. The doubts I had formerly gathered dissolved at once. When I looked at the cauldron, it had already grown dusty; because I was utterly without companions, I did not know how long it had been. That summer my brother Xuelang came north to see me; when he reached Mount Tai he could not hold back his grief, and after two nights he took his leave. In winter I built a plank hut to live in.
The Fourth Year, Bingzi (1576).

I was thirty-one. In the third month of spring Master Lianchi came to Mount Wutai on his travels and visited me, staying several days; at night we talked heart to heart and were much in accord. That year, after my awakening, there was no one from whom to seek instruction, so I opened the Lankavatara Sutra to verify it. I had never heard this sutra expounded and did not understand its meaning at all; so now I simply illumined it with direct perception. If a thought of the intellect stirred even slightly, it was not allowed to deliberate. Thus for eight months, and then the whole purport of the sutra was clear without doubt. In the seventh month of autumn Prefect Hu of Pingyang was transferred to Yanping as Military Defense Commissioner and came into the mountains to visit me. In my quiet room there was only oatmeal, wild greens and pickled vegetables. At that time the heat below was fierce, and his mounted attendants went to the ravine, broke ice and chewed it. The Duke saw it and said: This is another world. When I come here, my worldly thoughts are like this ice. In the tenth month of that winter, the abbot Dafang of Tayuan was falsely accused in a lawsuit; the circuit office proposed to repatriate and laicize him, and the monastery was nearly ruined. Chan Master Chekong of Mount Lu came and lived with me, and happened to see the affair, which grieved him greatly. I said: No harm will come of it. Thereupon I went in person to call on Duke Hu, braving heavy snow. When we met, Duke Hu said joyfully: I was just thinking how the heavy snow in the mountains must be hard to bear, and had written a letter to send someone to welcome you. Your coming is truly an answer to my feeling. In the end the abbot was released and the monastery preserved. He firmly kept me through the winter, questioning the Way morning and evening, and I spoke preliminary words for him. Duke Gao, the Supreme Commander, was transferred to garrison Daijun. Learning that I was in the yamen, he told Duke Hu: My family has a garden pavilion with many inscribed verses; I would like to ask a man of high attainment for a poem. Duke Hu agreed, and spoke to me. I said: There is not one word in my breast — how could I make a poem? I refused with all my might. So Duke Hu took a collection of ancient and modern poems and placed it on my table to stir my poetic thought. I happened to open it; just as I began to ponder, the mechanism suddenly stirred, and poetic lines came rushing beyond all checking. When Duke Hu came back from the hall, I had already set down twenty or thirty poems. I suddenly became aware and said: This is the demon of literary habit. I stopped at once and took one poem to fill the space. But the mechanism could not be stopped; unwittingly all the poetry, books, phrases and rhapsodies I had ever practiced, all that had ever entered my eyes, appeared at once and pressed and filled the empty sky. Even had my whole body been mouths, I could not have poured it all out. I no longer knew what was my body and mind. Silently I observed myself, on the verge of flying up, and there was nothing I could do. The next day, when Duke Hu had seen Duke Gao off, I sat alone and thought: This is exactly what Chan Master Faguang called the Chan sickness. Here, who can cure it for me? There is no way but that sound sleep may dissolve it. So I shut the door and forced myself to lie down. At first I could not; after a long while I sat forgetting and was as if asleep. The boy knocked at the door and could not open it; he pounded and got no answer. When Duke Hu returned he asked urgently, then had the window broken open, and saw me sitting upright wrapped in my robe. He called and got no answer; he shook me and I did not move. Earlier, in the study, there was a Buddha-offering table with a small gong. Duke Hu picked it up and asked: What is this for? I said: When monks of the Western Regions enter samadhi and cannot be awakened, this is sounded and they awaken. The Duke suddenly remembered this and said: Has the Master entered samadhi? He quickly took the gong and sounded it several tens of times by my ear. Only then did I slowly begin to wake. I opened my eyes and looked, and did not know where my body was. The Duke said: I left, and the Master shut the door and sat. It is five days now. I said: I did not know. It was a single breath. When I had spoken, I sat silently and examined closely, and in the end did not know where this was, nor whence I had entered. When I looked back on the mountains and on my former pilgrimage, each thing was a matter of dream. I sought them and could not find them; and all that had filled the sky with clamor was like rain scattered and clouds gathered, the long sky washed clean — all still, without a trace of image. Mind empty and realm still, its joy beyond all comparison. Then I said: When stillness is complete, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination the empty sky is contained. Then turning to look upon the world, it is as a matter in a dream. The Buddha's words truly did not deceive me. At the year's end, intending to return to the mountain at the New Year, I spoke to Duke Hu of how the forests of Mount Tai were being bitterly cut by wicked merchants, so that the bodhisattva's way-place would soon be bald and bare. The Duke prepared a memorial requesting a strict prohibition. Afterwards, when the state built monasteries, they all relied on the timber thus protected; otherwise there would have been no material to take.
The Fifth Year, Dingchou (1577).

I was thirty-two. That spring I returned from Yanmen. Thinking of my parents' boundless kindness, and mindful that I was much obstructed in the Dharma, I came upon the vow text of Master Nanyue Si and resolved to pierce my finger, take blood and mix it with gold to write out one copy of the great Flower Ornament Sutra, the Mahavaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra — above, to form a surpassing bond with prajñā; below, to requite boundless kindness. The design was conceived in the spring of that year. Earlier the Empress Dowager Cisheng had chosen monks to recite sutras for the protection of the state, and I had presumptuously been included in the list. Now, when she heard of the sutra-writing, she at once bestowed gold paper to aid it. The next year, in the fourth month, the writing of the sutra began. Master Chekong was traveling on Mount Kuang, and I wrote ten poems to see him off.
The Sixth Year, Wuyin (1578).

I was thirty-three, wholly bent on writing out the sutra. However large or small the stroke, at every stroke of the brush I spoke the Buddha's name once. Monks and laymen who came roaming the mountain I always had an attendant announce fully. Though my hand never ceased writing, I did not fail in my responses; whoever came to greet me I would exchange a few words with, and eminent men and old friends I would invite to sit on the meditation bed, talking with them without fail and without hindering the writing. Copying against the original, I made no error or omission. Each day was as usual, without the slightest sign of disturbance. The elders of the neighborhood secretly thought it strange and brought several crowds to test me, deliberately making a commotion. When the writing was done and read, it proved wholly reliable. So they asked Master Miao: How can Master Yin do this? Master Miao said: My friend has grown thoroughly familiar with this samadhi. From the time I dwelt on the mountain to the writing of the sutra, I had many auspicious dreams. One night I lodged and entered the Vajra Cave. On the stone gate was a placard: Great Prajñā Temple. Entering, I saw it vast as space, its halls and pavilions and towers adorned beyond compare. In the main hall there was only a great couch; I saw Great Master Qingliang reclining on the bed, with Master Miao standing in attendance on the left. I hurried in, bowed, and stood on the right. I heard the Great Master open and reveal the contemplation-realm of the perfect fusion of the first entry into the dharma-realm — that Buddha-lands enter into one another, host and companion interweave, and coming and going have no sign of motion. As he spoke the realm, it appeared before my eyes; and I knew my own body and mind interweaving and entering in. When he had finished, Master Miao asked: What realm is this? The Great Master laughed and said: The realm of no realm. When I awoke, I saw my own mind and realm fused and penetrating, without further doubt or obstruction. Another night I dreamed that I rose through space, higher and higher without limit. Descending, I saw the ten directions utterly void of anything, only a ground level as a mirror, pure as crystal. Far off I saw one vast tower, its measure like space. In the tower were all the people, things and undertakings of the world, down to the meanest market-town affairs, all contained within it, with no going out or coming in. In the tower was set a high seat, the color of purple-red flame; in my mind I called it the Vajra Jewel Seat. The tower's adornment was wonderful and inconceivable. I rejoiced and wished to draw near, but thought in my mind: How is it that in a pure realm there is this mixed filth? No sooner had the thought arisen than the tower receded. Then I thought again: Pure and impure arise from my own mind; and the tower came near again. After a moment I saw before the seat a company of monks standing in attendance, of lofty stature and incomparable dignity. Suddenly a young bhikshu came out from behind the seat, bearing a scroll of sutra, and coming down gave it to me, saying: The Elder is about to expound this sutra and has especially commanded that it be given to you. I took it and unrolled it; it was written in gold in Sanskrit letters that I did not know. So I wrapped it in my robes and asked who the Elder was. He said: Maitreya. I was glad, and followed the bhikshu upward. Reaching the tower's steps, I closed my eyes, gathered my thoughts and stood. Suddenly I heard the sound of a gong; I opened my eyes and saw that Maitreya had already ascended the seat. I at once looked up in reverence, and gazing at his face saw it gleaming with a purple-gold light, beyond compare in the world. When the homage was done, I thought: Now he speaks especially for me, so I am the one who fits the moment. So I knelt long, took up the scroll and unrolled it, and heard him say: Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Relying on consciousness, there is defilement; relying on wisdom, there is purity. Defilement has birth and death; purity has no Buddhas. At this my body and mind suddenly became like a dream, and I only heard the sounds in the air, clear and distinct, opening and brightening the ground of mind, with not one word retained. When I awoke, it was as if the words were still in my ear. From then on the division between consciousness and wisdom was clear in my mind and eye. And I knew that the place I had reached was the tower of Maitreya in the Tushita Heaven. Another night I dreamed that a monk came to announce: Bodhisattva Manjushri on the summit of the North Peak has prepared a bath and invites you. I followed and entered a vast hall filled with fragrance, its attendants all monks of the Western Regions, who led me to the bathhouse. I undid my clothes and entered the bath. I saw one person already in the pool; I looked and it was a woman. My mind was repelled and I did not wish to enter. The one in the pool deliberately floated his form, and I knew he was a man; so I entered and bathed with him. He scooped water with his hand and poured it over me from head downward, pouring into my five viscera like washing a barrel of meat. Each of the five viscera was rinsed clean without remainder, leaving only a skin like a crystal cage, thoroughly transparent. Then the one in the pool called for tea. I saw a monk of the Western Regions holding up half a skull, like a cut melon, and looking at it I saw the brains dripping; my mind greatly loathed it. The monk then dug with his finger and took some out, showing it to me and saying: Is this impure? At once he put it in his mouth and ate it. Thus he took and ate as he pleased, and it was sweet as honey. When the brains were all eaten, only blood and water remained. The one in the pool said: You may give it to him. The monk then gave it to me, and I took it and drank. Its taste was like sweet dew. I drank and it passed down through the pores of my body in a single flow. When I had finished, the monk of the Western Regions rubbed my back and gave a great slap with his palm; then I awoke. At that time my whole body streamed with sweat like water, and my five viscera were thoroughly clear. From then on body and mind were as if washed, light and joyful beyond compare. Dreams like these were mostly auspicious; in sum they were all exchanges with the sages. I often heard the Buddha's words; often there were such good dreams.
The Seventh Year, Jimao (1579).

I was thirty-four. In the autumn of that year the Great Cishou Temple of the capital was completed. At first the Empress Dowager, to make offerings for the late Emperor and protect the imperial person, wished to build the precious relic stupa of Tayuan Temple on Mount Wutai. She instructed the ministers, but they held that Mount Tai was too far from the capital, so a fortunate site near the capital was divined, and the Great Cishou Temple was built. That year the work was finished. When it was reported to the Empress Dowager, she felt that her vow regarding Mount Tai was not yet fulfilled, and instructed the Emperor to send palace officials with three thousand workmen and craftsmen to the mountain to build. At that time the court was only beginning to perform Buddhist works, and palace officials were being sent out for the first time; it was feared the work could not be completed and would injure the Dharma gate. I did my utmost to mediate and protect it, and from first to last there was no mishap.
The Eighth Year, Gengchen (1580).

I was thirty-five. That year there was a special decree to survey and measure the fields and grain of the realm, leaving not an inch of land out. Mount Tai had never been entered on the registers. Wicked men of the county, deceiving their superiors, wished to shift a grain quota of five hundred piculs onto Mount Tai, and repeatedly issued documents to investigate and report the land. In all the monasteries and quiet huts of the mountain there was not one man who could be at peace. From then on Mount Tai would have become a fox's den. The elders of the various temples gathered and told me. I calmed them, saying: You masters need not worry; let us take it slowly. Thereupon I sought means by circuitous ways and reported fully to the authorities, and in the end the survey was remitted, with not a pint or a peck added. Thus the way-places of Mount Tai were preserved whole.
The Ninth Year, Xinsi (1581).

I was thirty-six. That year we held the Unhindered Assembly. Earlier Master Miao too had written out the Flower Ornament Sutra in blood, sharing my vow; we wished to establish one perfect way-place called the Unhindered Assembly. Master Miao solicited donations, and the money and grain were all gathered. From the capital we invited five hundred greatly virtuous monks. All the arrangements for the way-place were complete. It happened that the Emperor had decreed prayers for an imperial heir, sending officials to Wudang, while the Empress Dowager sent officials to Wutai — to this very temple. I held that all Buddhist works done by monks are nothing but blessings for the state, secretly aiding the imperial rule. Now prayers for the imperial heir are the root of the state; nothing is greater than this. I wished to devote all the arrangements of the way-place we had prepared entirely to the single matter of praying for the heir, and not make it the name of one small self. Master Miao did not understand the idea; the palace envoys sent by the Emperor likewise did not understand the matter, having only flattery in mind. I strongly disapproved and contended for it, offending them; in the end my proposal was followed. Before long a rebel in Jiangnan made trouble, and those who disliked me wished to use this to slander me and destroy the way-place. Yet because of the cause of praying for the heir for the state, it was preserved whole, and from first to last there was no mishap. That year the stupa was completed, and I placed the gold-written Flower Ornament Sutra within the stupa repository, with a scroll of vow text. I myself solicited the making of a revolving canon of the Huazang world, and established a way-place within it. All the offerings, implements, vessels, vegetarian food, fruits and everything needed — Master Miao in the capital seemed to know nothing of it; I managed it all alone for ninety days and nights without my eyes closing. When the tenth month came, Master Miao led the five hundred and more monks he had invited; in one day they all assembled, a thousand people within and without. The arrangements for their lodging and the tea, rice and vegetarian meals were orderly without loss or confusion, and no one knew whence they came. Onlookers were all amazed. First we opened the Water and Land service for seven days and nights. For seven days I did not touch a grain of rice, only drinking water, yet the affairs were not neglected. Making offerings to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, we changed five hundred tables of offerings each day, in order without omission, and no one knew whence they came. Onlookers thought it divine transport; I too knew it was the Buddha's power added to us.
The Tenth Year, Renwu (1582).

I was thirty-seven. In the third month of that spring I expounded the Profound Discourse on the Flower Ornament Sutra. Within a hundred days the resident register reached a thousand, and monks and laymen gathered from the ten directions; each day there were no fewer than ten thousand. They ate as though seated in one hall, unmixed and unconfused, and no sound of calling or knocking was heard. I alone directed it all; there was no one else who could lift a finger. Even the wise did not know how it was so. The energy of my whole life was spent here. When the assembly ended in the third month, all that remained in the storehouse — money and grain of every kind, by estimate some ten thousand — I sealed and handed over entirely to the master of this temple as permanent property. Master Miao and I, with a single bowl, drifted away. Master Miao went to Luya, while I, being ill, went to Zhangshiyan in Zhending to recuperate. I wrote one poem, with the lines: The sheer cliffs pierce the sky and should narrow the sun; the broken crag has no road, only a flying ladder. In the eighth month of that year an imperial prince was born. I again went to Zhongfeng Temple west of the capital and wrote a preface to the recarved Extensive Record of Zhongfeng, spending the winter in water-fasting in a stone chamber.
The Eleventh Year, Guiwei (1583).

I was thirty-eight. In the first month of spring the water fast ended. But because of the empty reputation of Mount Tai — it is said that beneath a great name it is hard to dwell long — I went to the shores of the Eastern Sea and first changed my name to Hanshan. From then on I no longer knew that there was a Cheng Yin. At first, because of the fire at this temple I was determined to restore it, and so practiced to limit conditions. But my eight years on Mount Tai had many opportunities, and I feared to lose the time from afar; therefore I hid on the Eastern Sea. This was my original mind. In the fourth month of summer, on the eighth day, I reached Mount Lao. When Master Miao first took leave of me, because I could not travel alone he assigned his Dharma kinsman Dezong to be my attendant. I had first read in the Chapter on the Dwellings of Bodhisattvas in the Flower Ornament Sutra Commentary: In the Eastern Sea there is a place named the Nārāyaṇa Cave, where from ancient times hosts of bodhisattvas have dwelt. The Qingliang Commentary says: In Sanskrit nārāyaṇa means firm and solid; that is Mount Lao by the Eastern Sea. In the Tribute of Yu it is within the borders of Deng and Lai in Qingzhou. Today the cave still exists there. I admired it, and so made a special visit to Mount Lao. I found the place indeed, but it was uninhabitable; so I explored the deepest recess of the southern slope, backed by a host of mountains and facing the swallowing sea — utterly wonderful, truly not a place of the human world. The site was called Guanyin Hermitage, an ancient temple of which only the ruined foundation remained. On inquiry, it was where, at the beginning of the Yuan, the Seven Perfected Ones arose in the east and, borrowing the power and favor of Emperor Shizu, seized many Buddhist temples and changed them into Daoist cloisters. When Shizu returned from his western campaign, the monks memorialized, and many were ordered restored; only Mount Lao, secluded by the sea, had not been reached. I rejoiced in the place's seclusion — truly a spot to flee the world and cut off men. I vowed to dwell there. At first I spread a mat under a tree for seven months. Afterwards I found the local layman Zhang Daxin, who cut thatch and built me a hut to live in. In my first year on the mountain no one came or went, and my mind was greatly at ease. At that time there was Dharma Master Guifeng of Lingshan Temple in Jimo, an eye of that region, and I rejoiced to be with him.
The Twelfth Year, Jiashen (1584).

I was thirty-nine. In the seventh month of autumn the Empress Dowager, because of the labor of our prayers for an heir at Wutai, sought out the three who had been in charge — Dafang, Miaofeng and myself. The other two masters had already arrived and received her gifts; only I could not be found, and she sought me with all her might. So she ordered my former host, the abbot Rui'an of Longhua Temple, to seek me in person. Learning that I was by the sea, he came on foot with staff, and declared the compassionate decree. I earnestly declined, saying: If I may receive the holy grace of being allowed to grow old among mountains and seas, I have received more than enough; what else should I seek? When he reported back, the holy intention would not cease, and soon a site was divined west of the capital for a temple, and a palace envoy was sent to fix a time and insist that I come. In the end I declined and did not go. The envoy reported back my firm resolve to lie hidden in the mountains. The holy mind pitied me, and asking whether I had no dwellings, at once issued three thousand in gold, again sending the former envoy to deliver it for building a hermitage. When it arrived I firmly stopped him, saying: My few thatched rafters are more than enough joy; what use is much? The envoy pressed me and dared not report back. I said: The ancients had the case of forging a decree to relieve famine. Now Shandong has a bad year; why not spread the holy compassion to the starving? So I had the monks lead the envoy to distribute it among the monks, Daoists, orphans, elders and prisoners of every prefecture, taking the sealed registers of each office in receipt. The holy heart was greatly pleased and sighed in admiration without cease. Later, when I met with trouble and was handed to the Zhenfu office, they interrogated me about several uses of the inner treasury gold; I answered by asking them to check the inner treasury's disbursement registers. On checking, there was only this one matter of relieving famine; not a hair besides. In the end the imperial displeasure was resolved.
The Thirteenth Year, Yiyou (1585).

I was forty. The people of the east had never known monks. When I dwelt in the mountains, the Huang clan was the greatest, and its sons gradually drew near. The man now called the heretic Luo Qing was a man of Chengyang below the mountain — the very birthplace of the heresy — and so his teaching spread everywhere in the east, and the Three Treasures were utterly unknown. Dwelling here, I gradually gathered and converted them. After a long time, all who had been teachers among them led their followers to submit. From then on they first knew that there was a Buddhadharma. This was the beginning of my founding work.
The Fourteenth Year, Bingxu (1586).

I was forty-one. That year the canon was distributed. At the founding of the dynasty the canon had been carved, but writings of this land that had not been included were now, by order of the Empress Dowager, to be added. When the carving was complete, the Emperor decreed the distribution of fifteen canons to famous mountains throughout the realm. First, four copies were given to the four frontiers: Mount Lao by the Eastern Sea, Putuo by the Southern Sea, Emei in western Shu, and Luya on the northern border. At that time the Empress Dowager, because of the Mount Tai affair, summoned me several times, but I did not know it and did not accept the gifts. So one copy of the canon was sent first to the Eastern Sea, though at first I did not know it. When it reached Mount Lao there was nowhere to install it, and the grand coordinators and censors had the local offices make offerings. Seeing that there was an imperial decree, I went to the capital to give thanks. Then the holy compassion was extended: all the palace household was ordered to give alms to build a temple and install the canon in offering, and the name Haiyin Temple was requested and granted. While in the capital I heard that Chan Master Daguan had come seeking me by the sea, so I hurried back and traveled by forced stages to overtake him. It happened that the Master had left the mountain, and soon we returned together. We lingered twenty days, and he gave me a poem with the lines: At leisure you came to dwell above the sea; your name has strayed and fallen on Shandong. In the eleventh month of that winter — from the year Xinsi onward I had been mostly toiling and had never been able to rest, and so was often weary — now that the meditation hut was at last finished I could settle in peace. Body and mind were let go, and the joy was beyond compare. One night as I sat in stillness and rose in the night, I saw the sea limpid and the sky clear, snow and moon exchanging light. Suddenly body, mind and world sank level in that instant, like the shadows of flowers in the sky falling away; thoroughly there was one great treasury of radiance, utterly without a thing. Then I spoke a verse: The sea limpid, the sky clear, the light of snow and moon; herein the ordinary and the sage cut off all going and hiding. The vajra eye breaks through, the sky-flowers fall; the whole great earth returns to the ground of extinction. I went back into my room and took up the Surangama Sutra to verify it. Opening the scroll I saw: Your body and your mind, and the mountains, rivers, space and the great earth without, are all things within the wonderful, bright, true mind. Then the whole sutra's contemplative realm was clear in my mind and eye. At once I took up my brush and composed one scroll of the Surangama Hanging Mirror; before half a candle had burned it was done. At that time the meditation hall had just begun its quiet sitting, so I called the keeper of discipline into my room and had him read it to me. It was as if I heard words in a dream.
The Fifteenth Year, Dinghai (1587).

I was forty-two. That year I built the halls and first opened the hall to expound the precepts for the assembly. From then on monks came from the four directions in increasing numbers. For laymen I wrote the Direct Explanation of the Heart Sutra. In the autumn of that year Censor-in-Chief Hu asked leave to return to his fields, and brought his own son, whom he gave to leave home as my attendant, naming him Fushan.
The Sixteenth Year, Wuzi (1588).

I was forty-three. At that time students read my Surangama Hanging Mirror and asked: This sutra's mind-contemplation is fully clear, but it has not wholly dissolved the words and phrases, and later students may find it hard to enter. We beg you to dissolve every word and phrase back into the contemplation of mind; that would be a gift of Dharma beyond measure. So I first conceived the idea of composing a Comprehensive Commentary. I had already established its main purport, but had not yet set it to draft.
The Seventeenth Year, Jichou (1589).

I was forty-four. That year I read the canon and expounded for the assembly the Lotus Sutra and the Awakening of Faith. Since leaving Wutai I had often had the thought of visiting my parents, and I feared falling into worldly truth; so I tested myself. One night as I sat in stillness, I suddenly opened my eyes and there was a verse: Day after day mist and waves soak the cold sky; fish and birds roam together in one mirror. Last night the moon beyond the sky suddenly sank; its lone brightness must be mingled with the black dragon's. Then I urgently called my attendant and said: Now I may return to my old home and see my two elders. Earlier I had begged for one copy of the Great Canon for Bao'en Temple. In the tenth month of winter I reached the capital to request the canon, and the Emperor at once ordered it sent with an escort. In the eleventh month I reached Longjiang and this temple. The precious stupa emitted light for many days. On the day of welcoming the sutras, the stupa's light was like a bridge, and the monks walked within the light as they welcomed the canon facing north. When the sutras were installed and the way-place established, the light did not cease day after day. Those who came to bow and revere numbered more than ten thousand a day, and they took it for a rare auspicious sign. My old mother, hearing that I had come, first sent someone to ask on what day I would reach home. I said: I act for the court's affairs, not for my family. If my old mother can see me and be as joyful as if we had never parted, I can stay but two nights; otherwise I shall not return. When my old mother heard this she said: To meet again alive, the joy is endless; how could there be sorrow? One meeting is enough — why speak of two nights? When I returned, my old mother saw me and was so overjoyed she nearly fell over. I thought it most strange. That night as we sat, an elder of the clan asked whether I had come by boat or by land. My old mother answered at once: Why ask whether by boat or by land? The questioner said: From where have you come? My old mother said: From the sky. I was startled and said: No wonder the old woman could let me go in those days. Then I asked my old mother: Since we parted, did you think of me? She said: How could I not think of you? I asked: How did you console yourself? She said: At first I did not know. When I learned you were on Mount Wutai, I asked the masters where Mount Wutai was. They said: Beneath the Northern Dipper — that is where your son dwells. From then on each night I bowed to the Northern Dipper and called the bodhisattva's name, and so thought of you no more. And now, thinking you dead, I neither bowed nor thought of you at all. Now I see you — you have come as a manifestation. The next day I sacrificed at the ancestral graves, and divined a burial site for my two parents. My old father was then eighty. I joked: Today I shall bury the old man alive, to save coming again another day. I lifted the mattock to break the ground; my old mother snatched it, saying: The old woman will bury herself — why trouble anyone? She struck several tens of blows in a row. On the third day I took my leave; my old mother was joyful as ever and never once frowned. Only then did I know that my old mother was no ordinary woman. In Jimo there was a certain Huang Nashan, styled Ziguang, younger brother of the present Grand Minister. When I first came to the sea he was nineteen; at once he took refuge, sought instruction, and I gave him the Surangama Sutra; in two months he could recite it. From then on he kept vegetarian, and though his parents reproached him his mind did not change. He was wholly set on investigating, and his side never touched the mat. When I was returning south, Guang thought to himself: I was born in a border land and for kalpas have not heard the names of the Three Treasures. Now happily I have met a great good friend who is a friend unasked. If he does not return, we shall lose our reliance. So before the Great Being Guanyin he cut his arm and lit a lamp in offering, praying that the Great Being would keep me and bring me back soon. Afterwards the burn ached; day and night he sat upright, holding the name of the Great Being Guanyin, and in three months he was healed. When healed he saw that the scar had formed the image of the Great Being, brows, eyes, body and robes, as clear as a painting. Even his mother and wife did not know. He constantly sought to leave home, but I would never permit it. Then he said: If your disciple turns a somersault, how can the Master stop me? Thus one knows that even in the land of the mlecchas the Buddha-seed is never cut off. At first, because of restoring this temple, I intended to dwell on Mount Tai, and the affair already had prospects; but since the cost would run to several hundred thousand, it was not easy to raise, so I waited for the time by the sea. Now the time was nearly ripe, and I took the occasion of delivering the canon to return to the southern capital. Having learned the whole story of this temple, I returned and reported it fully in memorial to the Empress Dowager, saying: The work is great and the cost immense, hard to undertake lightly. I beg that the Empress Dowager reduce her daily delicacies by a hundred taels; accumulated over three years the matter can be undertaken, and in ten years the work can be completed. The holy heart was greatly pleased, and ordered the accumulation to begin in the twelfth month of that year.
The Eighteenth Year, Gengyin (1590).

I was forty-five. That year the halls were completed. In spring I wrote out the Lotus Sutra on behalf of the Empress Dowager. At that time local officials wished to scheme for the way-place; they stirred up a Daoist priest from beyond the pale, falsely claiming that it occupied their cloister, and gathered many people to bring suit at the governor's yamen. Duke Li, the Supreme Commander, had already learned the whole matter and bitterly hated it, so he sent it down to Laizhou Prefecture to be thoroughly investigated. I attended the hearing in person and did my utmost to save them. Several hundred rascals made an uproar in the prefectural city, and there was a ring of men about me. At that time I had two attendants with me; I sent them off elsewhere and walked slowly alone among them. The ringleader held a bronze plaque, and a sharp blade came out of its sheath. He danced before me, meaning to kill me. I looked at him laughing and said: If you kill a man, how will you answer for yourself? The man's spirit faltered; he put away the plaque and knife. They escorted me about two li outside the city, and were about to part ways, when the mad crowd suspected that their leader had been bribed by me and wanted to beat him. I silently reckoned that if the crowd once roused, the man would be in danger. What was to be done? So as we hesitated at parting, I seized the leader and brought him with me to my lodging. I shut the door, took off my outer robe, sat at ease and talked and laughed as usual, taking melons and fruit for us to eat together. At that time the whole market was clamoring: The Daoist has killed the monk! When the prefect heard it he at once sent many runners to arrest them. The crowd was frightened and all knocked their heads, begging to be excused. I said: Fear not, and do not argue; only hear what I say. When they arrived, the prefect asked: Have the madmen killed the monk? I said: Not yet. When you came to arrest them, this monk was just eating melons and fruit with their leader. The prefect said: Why did they make an uproar? I said: The market's noise. The prefect wanted to put them in the cangue. I said: I am about to disperse them; the cangue would only hold them fast. The prefect understood, and ordered the local authorities to drive them all away. Within three days the mad crowd had all dispersed. Thereupon the matter was settled. That year I wrote the Treatise on the Influence of the Old Master and Zhuangzi.
The Nineteenth Year, Xinmao (1591).
I was forty-six. That year the Empress Dowager made a sandalwood image of Vairocana Buddha and built the great hall. In the autumn of that year my disciple Huang Ziguang passed away sitting.
The Twentieth Year, Renchen (1592).

I was forty-seven. In the seventh month of that autumn I went to the capital and visited Chan Master Daguan at Shangfang. In the Jin dynasty there was Duke Wan, who, fearing that the three disasters would destroy the kalpa and with it the Buddhadharma, carved the stone sutras and stored them in stone chambers. His stupa courtyard had been sold by monks, and the Master redeemed it and wished me to write a record of it. I happened to arrive, and the Master was overjoyed. When we met we went together to Mount Shijing, and I wrote the Record of Duke Wan's Stupa Courtyard and the Record of the Reburial of the Relics, as well as the earlier Haiyin Drafts. At that time I lingered with Master Da in each other's company for forty days and nights, a wonder of my life.
The Twenty-First Year, Guisi (1593).

I was forty-eight. That year Shandong suffered a great famine and the dead filled the roads. All the vegetarian grain stored in the mountains I distributed to relieve the people near the mountain, and when that was not enough I took passage on convenient boats to Liaodong and bought several hundred piculs of beans to relieve them. Thus among the people of the four communities of the border mountains, not one died of hunger.
The Twenty-Second Year, Jiawu (1594).

I was forty-nine. In the third month of spring that year Duke Zheng Kunya, the Supreme Commander of Shandong, entered the mountains to visit me and ask about the Dharma, and I spoke expedient words for him. In the tenth month of winter I went to the capital to offer congratulations on the imperial birthday, and stayed there over the New Year. I was asked to expound the precepts at Cishou Temple. At that time, because of the cause of restoring this temple, I knew the Empress Dowager's accumulation was already substantial, so I asked that the work be begun. But the Emperor, because the Japanese had invaded Korea, was then deliberating a punitive expedition, so it was left for later and the plan was shelved.
Dream-Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Fifty-Four.

blocks.text: Old Man Hanshan's Autobiographical Chronology, Part Two

inline.s: The Twenty-Third Year, Yiwei (1595).

I was fifty. In the first month of spring I returned to the sea from the capital, and at once met with calamity. Originally, when the canon was issued by imperial order, palace envoys were sent to deliver it to four places, and those men had first reached the Eastern Sea. Earlier the Emperor, sparing expense, had always disliked the palace envoys for requesting funds for Buddhist works too often. At that time someone in the inner court happened to offend the imperial anger over another matter, and it was about to reach the Empress Dowager; the ministers on left and right were alarmed. It also happened that an influential palace officer bore a grudge against the envoy who delivered the sutras and wished him dead, and so took the occasion to start trouble. He made use of the earlier rumors of the Daoist priest and had the Eastern Depot's agents dress as Daoists and strike the drum of appeal to present a memorial. When the Emperor read it he was greatly enraged and ordered an arrest. Because of the cause of delivering the sutras, I too was implicated. When I heard the report I said to the assembly: The Buddha, for the sake of one being, does not abandon the three evil paths. Now this land of the Eastern Sea is a land of mlecchas, where the names of the Three Treasures were never heard. Now I have taught and converted here for twelve years, and three-year-old children all know to recite the Buddha's name. As for those who abandon the false and return to the true, they are found in village after village and household after household. My vow is fulfilled; what regret is there in death? Only the vow to restore this temple is unfulfilled, and that pains my heart. So I left Jimo. The scholars and townsfolk, old and young, came out of the whole city, weeping and following me to see me off — enough to show how deeply men's hearts had been moved. When I reached the capital I received the decree handing me to the Zhenfu office for interrogation. The officials in charge had first received hints of the imperial wish and wanted me to confess everything and implicate all the funds given by the Empress Dowager to the various famous mountains, no less than several hundred thousand in all. They tortured me cruelly. I said: I am ashamed to be a monk and have no way to repay the state's kindness. How should I now begrudge one death and wound the Emperor's great filial piety? To twist the truth and falsely confess in order to seize profit, to obey the imperial wish and so damage the moral order, is by no means the heart of a subject who loves his lord. What of the historians' verdict? With all my strength I resisted, confessing only the earlier seven hundred odd pieces of gold given by the public. When the Emperor checked the inner disbursement ledgers, and the registers of the earlier famine relief in Shandong, the imperial displeasure was resolved. Thereupon mother and son were as before. Then sentence was proposed, and by holy grace, having taken pity and examined the matter, I was sentenced for privately founding a monastery and sent into exile at Leizhou. I was imprisoned in the third month of that year. All the temples of the capital recited sutras and performed repentance for my protection; among the monks some burned incense and scorched their arms, kept water fasts and recited spells to add their protection. Zheng, the Grand Marshal of Ansu, and the son of Duke Fanxi, then in the imperial guard, though we had never met, specially prepared a banquet and gathered the officials at court to beg for my rescue, even to tears, pleading my innocence. So deeply did men's hearts act for the Dharma at that time. I was in prison eight months, and the only one who brought me food was my attendant Fushan. In the tenth month of winter I was sent south. Many officials and scholars, in plain clothes and on weak donkeys, came to see me off and help me cross. On the day I left the capital, Fushan followed with two or three monks. In the eleventh month I reached Nanjing, and on the river took leave of my old mother, writing for her the Mother and Son Inscription, and brought with me my orphaned nephew Kejiu. Earlier, with Master Daguan on Mount Shijing, I had thought how desolate the Chan gate was, and said that Caoxi was the source of Chan; surely the source must be choked, and I resolved to go there with him to clear it. Master Da had gone ahead and waited for me at Mount Kuang. When I met with trouble the Master was living at Tianchi; hearing the report he was greatly shocked and said: Hanshan is finished, and the vow of Caoxi is unfulfilled. So the Master went first to Caoxi, and on the way back at Liaocheng heard that I was about to be sent out, and so returned to Jinling to wait. When I arrived we took leave of each other in the Lübodu Hut on the river. The Master wished to strive to clear me of the false charge. I said: The command of ruler and father, and the service of subject and son, are not different; and what of fixed karma? I beg the Master not to speak of it. At the parting of the ways we grasped each other's arms, and he said: When I heard of your trouble at Tianchi, I vowed before the Buddha to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times to keep you from harm. My heart is your tongue. I only bowed in thanks and took my leave. The Master wrote for me his Discourse on Expelling the Guest.
The Twenty-Fourth Year, Bingshen (1596).

I was fifty-one. In the first month of spring I passed through Wenjiang and visited the Remonstrating Censor Zou Nangao. Wang Xinghai, a grand traveler of Luling, paid his respects to me on the river and asked me to write a commentary on the Lankavatara Sutra. In the second month I crossed Yu Ridge and, at its head, saw the place where Huiming seized the robe; I wrote a poem in lament, with the lines: Turning over in thought the night-traveler of former days — how does he compare with today's heart crossing the ridge? Seeing the road so rugged and travelers sweating blood, I assigned a monk to set up a free-tea hermitage at the ridge's head, and a Daoist urged the repair of the road, which in a few years became a level highway. At Shaoyang I entered the mountains and paid my respects to the Patriarch, and drank the water of Caoxi. My verse: The drop of Caoxi water comes from the spirit source; it flows into the dark sea, waves beating the sky. How many fish and dragons have transformed therein? The single vein of the source is still clear and cold. Seeing that the Patriarch's court was in decline beyond words, I left in sorrow. Reaching Wuyang, I saw the General in prison clothes. The General had my bonds loosed, and entertained me with a vegetarian meal; I lodged at Haizhu Temple. Duke Zhou Haimen, a great counselor, came to visit with several tens of his students. As we sat, Duke Zhou raised the question: Understanding the way of day and night, and thereby knowing. Among the crowd an elder who called himself an old practitioner answered: Everyone has knowing and awareness; when busy with affairs by day it is this knowing, and when dreaming by night it is also this knowing. Therefore it is said: understanding the way of day and night, and thereby knowing. Duke Zhou said: All the assembly says the same, yet in my mind it is not necessarily so. Then he asked me: Old Chan Master, pray instruct us. I said: From what classic does this saying come? The Duke said: From the Appended Phrases of the Book of Changes. He recited several lines in succession. I said: This is the sage pointing out to men that they must awaken to that one thing which does not belong to birth and death. Duke Zhou struck the table and said: The old Chan Master has indeed pointed it out intimately. All were bewildered, and asked again. Duke Zhou said: Birth and death are the way of night and day; to understand night and day is to no longer belong to night and day. The whole assembly sighed in admiration. Earlier the various protectors of the Dharma had written to the Grand Marshal Duke Chen at the military headquarters, who sent travel warrants and help across. On the tenth day of the third month I reached Leizhou and was enrolled in the ranks, lodging at an old temple west of the city. On the first day of the fourth month of summer I began writing my commentary on the Lankavatara Sutra. At that time there was a great famine, pestilence broke out everywhere, and it had not rained for a year; the dead and injured were beyond words. I sat as if in a charnel grove, sustaining it by the power of Dharma, at peace. In the drought the well water dried up; only the good attendant Shan followed me. Every midnight we would get one jar of water to last the day. Starving men looked at it, and to get one drop was like sweet dew from heaven. Within and without the city, bones lay exposed. In the seventh month of autumn I and the licentiate Ke Shifu urged the people to gather them, and the bones and skeletons we buried numbered ten thousand. Then we held a service of deliverance, and at once it rained heavily, three feet of water on level ground; from then on the pestilential air dispersed. In the eighth month the garrison headquarters summoned me back to Wuyang and housed me at the military training ground; at that time I came and went and wrote twenty poems On Following the Army. On first passing the Bitter Vine of Dianbai, the gate of the ridge bandits, I wrote an inscription and built a free-tea hermitage. Ding Youwu, a great counselor of Yuzhang, arrived, exiled to Guanghai on a false charge; we had long admired each other, and so became inseparable friends.
The Twenty-Fifth Year, Dingyou (1597).

I was fifty-two. In the first month of spring, when many in the provincial city had died and bones lay exposed, I had people gather and bury them, also numbering several thousand, and held a Universal Deliverance service for seven days and nights. Ding Youwu assisted in person. Earlier the Cantonese had not known the Buddha; from then on they joyfully turned to take refuge. In the fourth month of summer my Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra were finished. Since some of the scholars who had taken refuge had not entered the Buddha's teaching, I wrote the Direct Pointing at the Doctrine of the Mean to draw them out. At first those above and below saw me as a criminal monk and took me very lightly. Duke Chen Rugang, the Grand Marshal at the military headquarters, was extremely strict in law, and none dared visit him privately; I did not go to see him, yet he sent people to inquire after me most solicitously. In the ninth month of that year I went with Youwu to call on him. When we reached the gate and announced ourselves, he stopped us. That evening he came in person to bow to me on the boat, bringing a tea box, and sat in talk until the third watch; all were amazed. Afterwards he praised me greatly to the authorities, saying: He is a phoenix among monks. He instructed even the three provincial offices to go and bow to me. From then on everyone knew that monks were to be esteemed.
The Twenty-Sixth Year, Wuxu (1598).

I was fifty-three. In the first month of spring Censor Fan Youxuan, for his views on establishing the heir, was exiled to Leizhou. He first visited me at Wuyang, when I was collating my Lankavatara draft. The Duke asked me what the scenery of Leiyang was like. I picked up the scroll of the sutra and showed it to him, saying: This is the scenery of Leiyang. The Duke sighed in wonder, and at once wrote a solicitation for its carving. Duke Zhou Haimen, when he held office as judge of Guangdong, came and went asking after the Way; later, in charge of Nan Shao, he assigned me to compile the Caoxi Gazetteer. The scholars of Guangdong had not known the Buddha; when Duke Zhou expounded Wang Yangming's learning he gathered the scholars and had them ask me about the Way. There was a certain Long Zhang, who, hearing my discourse, was struck by it, and going home told his friends Wang Anshun and Feng Changli: We have heard that a Chan master from the north expounds the Dharma most wonderfully. Both came to seek instruction. I opened to them the upward matter; they believed without doubt and were wholly set on investigation. Both had long been virtuous, and they led others to take refuge, so the numbers grew daily. From then on they first knew that there were Buddha, Dharma and Sangha. After this the Dharma teaching opened wide; it was the strength of these three. Often recalling Master Da's vow about the sutra, that summer I first built a meditation hall among the ramparts, intending to imitate Dahui's teaching in cap and kerchief. So I gathered Dharma companions who had come from afar, and the disciples beneath the bodhi tree at Faxing Temple — Tong'an, Chaoyi, Tongjiong and several tens of others — and recited the Lotus Sutra, and expounded it for the assembly. When we came to the Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa, I suddenly awakened to the Buddha's meaning and its essential point: that for every person in this Saha world, what lies before their eyes is the Huazang world. Yet it requires three transformations only because of those of inferior faculties, showing them a single glimpse by degrees. The ancients took the last six chapters as circulation, and did not see the Buddha's meaning either. So I wrote my Rhythmic Beats on the Lotus Sutra. Youwu was by nature impetuous and vehement, and full of generosity; he knew to respect monks but did not know the Buddhadharma. When he was about to return, I saw him off on the boat and gave him a heavy hammering; the Duke suddenly awakened. So I gave him the style Juefei, Layman Who Has Awakened to What Is Not, and gave him an inscription, and also wrote the Inscription on Clarifying the Mind to warn him.
The Twenty-Seventh Year, Jihai (1599).

I was fifty-four. In spring the carving of my Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra was finished. I expounded it once for the assembly, printed more than a hundred copies, and sent them everywhere to the wise of the Dharma gate throughout the land and to the officials who protected the Dharma, so that they might know that even amid hardship I had not forgotten the Buddha's work. The customs of Guangdong were much given to killing; at the Ghost Festival all killed living beings to sacrifice to their ancestors. At that time the markets piled up livestock like firewood — a most pitiful sight. So I held the Ullambana Assembly and expounded the Commentary on the Balance of Filial Piety, urging that on that day one should feed monks, release living creatures and sacrifice with vegetables. Many followed. From then on, at all great matters of mourning and sacrifice, on parents' birthdays, or in prayers for deliverance, people bowed in repentance, released life and kept vegetarian. Before long there were life-releasing societies everywhere. It was one turning point in the Dharma's transformation of the people. In the fifth month of summer that year Duke Chen, Grand Marshal at the military headquarters, was transferred to garrison the provincial city. When he first alighted from his carriage he did not bow to a single local official, but first sent to inquire after me. Soon after he ordered food vessels, more than a hundred pieces, all of the finest, and none of his household knew what they were for. When the vegetarian feast was set, he asked me out specially and brought out the new vessels. Everyone then knew how highly he esteemed me. Before long he asked leave to return home. In the autumn of that year the tax commissioners went out everywhere, and local affairs multiplied daily from then on. Duke Yang Fusuo, Junior Steward of Huizhou, had long been deeply in accord with me in the Dharma gate; he had returned home in mourning, and in that autumn I went to visit him. On the day I arrived, the Duke had already died at his grave site; at dawn, as I was about to enter the mountains, his coffin had already reached the city. So I went to attend the dressing of the corpse and to seek coffin and outer coffin. It happened that I met the Circuit Observer Ren of Chaoyang Road, who was at Huiyang on direct commission; he invited me to tour West Lake and to climb Dongpo's White Crane Peak, and then I returned. Once back, I wished to shut my gate and sweep away the world.
The Twenty-Eighth Year, Gengzi (1600).

I was fifty-five. At that time the tax commissioners had just come out, fierce, violent and overbearing; officials and people could not bear it, and the region was shaken. Added to this were alarms of Japanese pirates, and men's hearts were in panic. So I dispersed my disciples and shut my gate, cutting off all traces. The Cantonese had long suffered from the white-sailed boats of the Fujian sea carrying rice, and feared the price would soar; at that time they took it for rebellion. The new military commissioner was a man of Fujian, and his son's boat was anchored at sea. It happened that the General had asked leave and was about to depart, and the tax commissioner was nursing a design against him. There happened to be several white-sailed boats, and he seized on this as a pretext, claiming the General had supplied the commissioner's son with passage. He incited the townspeople to a great uproar; in a moment several thousand gathered, throwing bricks and stones. They nearly broke the son's boat, besieged the general's residence, and brandished spears at him in great urgency. At that time the three provincial offices and the prefecture and county were all at the military headquarters offering seasonal greetings, and there was not one ranking official in the provincial city; in the end there was no one to rescue him. The turn of events hung on a breath. The General, in danger, had no recourse but to order his central army to come before my gate to beg for deliverance. I firmly refused, saying: I have no divine art. The central army knelt in tears and said: If the Master does not think of host and guest, will he not think of the living people of this region? Hearing this I was alarmed, and so opened my gate and went to call on the tax commissioner, calmly persuading and converting him and opening his understanding. Hearing my words the commissioner indeed awakened, and ordered them to pacify themselves and so disperse the rioters. I went first, and cried out to the crowd: What you gentlemen do now is to get cheap rice. Now you have broken the great law and deserve death; even if there were cheap rice, who would eat it? Hearing this the crowd was stunned. Presently the order reached the general's residence, and the siege was lifted. Thus the provincial city was at peace. The elders were grateful to me and wished to make offering to me as to a guardian spirit. At that time the three offices were dining at the military headquarters; hearing the report that the people were rioting, they all threw down their chopsticks and rose. When they returned, all was already settled; yet all knew it was my doing. When the Circuit Observer Ren heard of it, he sent me a letter saying: If Master Hanshan does not come out, what will become of the region? And now that Master Hanshan has come out, what will become of Master Hanshan? I too knew that from then on there would be no peaceful days. In the autumn of that year the Circuit Commissioner Zhu of Nan Shao invited me to enter Caoxi. I went into the mountains on the impulse, to be a slave-servant of the Sixth Patriarch. The new Governor-General Dai, learning that I had pacified the rioters, was deeply grateful and wished to see me once; he instructed the General to bring me to call on him. When we met, his courtesy was most generous, and he kept me to a vegetarian meal. So I took leave to go to Caoxi, and the Duke then vowed to be my protector of the Dharma. Thereby I gained peace of mind.
The Twenty-Ninth Year, Xinchou (1601).

I was fifty-six. In the first month of spring I looked at Caoxi and saw rogues from every quarter gathered at the mountain gate, opening butcher shops and wine stalls, a most foul defilement whose accumulated abuse was more than a hundred years old. Graves encroached on the Patriarch's mountain, monks' property was much seized, and they joined with outside rogues to swindle the temple monks; none dared look them in the face. I sighed and said: This is a disease of the heart and belly. If it is not removed, the way-place of the Sixth Patriarch will in the end become a fox's den, and there will be no saving it. What would I be doing dwelling here? After deep and unending thought, I went and told Governor-General Dai. The Duke said: No difficulty. Let me try to carry it out for you with all my strength. At once he ordered the county to stand guard and within three days drive them all out, not leaving one man; the shops were all torn down, not a tile left. From then on the accumulated filth of Caoxi's mountain gate was washed away in a single morning. The Duke then kept me to a vegetarian meal and sat in talk. He said: I have washed away the stench of the Sixth Patriarch for you. But now the living people of the region are plunged in misery — what compassion has the great bodhisattva to save them? I said: What do you mean? The Duke said: A thousand pearl boats are all great pirates of the sea. Now, under the authority of the imperial requisition, they are given power; when the requisition ends they do not return but run amok at sea, plundering without end, and the law cannot stop them. This is one. Then there is mining in the region: the corvée laborers are violent and overbearing, digging up men's graves and ruining their property; everywhere the common people suffer its poison worse than plunder, and so the people have no rest. What is to be done? I said: This is not easy to speak of. Let us consider it slowly. The requisition commissioner Li had considerable faith. In the autumn of that year he came to Caoxi to offer incense to the Sixth Patriarch and stayed in the mountains several days; hearing the Dharma he was much pleased. So I urged him to be the gold-giving benefactor for the revival of the Patriarch's court, and he generously took it up. Then I quietly and secretly opened to him: The mining does great harm to the region, and it is not the sage Emperor's intention.
